Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 312, to amend the Supreme Court Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that this
bill was framed for the purpose of obviating a difficulty which might arise upon the retirement of Mr. Justice Mignault which is to take place on September 30 next, under the provisions of an act which was passed by this house a few sessions ago, making retirement compulsory at the age of 75 years. I wish simply to express my personal opinion that despite the general grounds presented to the house when the act for compulsory retirement was passed, probably no man on the supreme court bench of Canada is better qualified, physically and intellectually, to perform the functions of his office than is Mr. Justice Mignault. Personally, I think it is a public misfortune that his compulsory retirement is necessary at this time, and I desire to give expression to a view which I have heard expressed in the province of which I have the honour to be one of the representatives, to this effect: In case a judge has been appointed for life it is a serious breach of contract when that judge is compelled to retire at an age and at a time when he is thoroughly equipped, physically and intellectually, for the performance of his judicial duties, and especially in view of the fact that his compulsory retirement necessitates his taking a pension which is very considerably less than the salary which would otherwise be paid to him under his contract with the state. I am simply giving expression to a view which I think is generally
prevalent among the legal fraternity in my province, that in Mr. Justice Mignault's case there should be some exceptional consideration given by the government to the fact that he is retired by an act of parliament which is in apparent breach of his contract with the state, and he is thereby compelled to accept a pension which is much less than he would otherwise have received, and at a time when he is physically and intellectually competent to perform his judicial duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, this bill is
general in its character and does not apply to any special case. With regard to the act passed two years ago, parliament in its wisdom thought it well to fix an age limit so far as federal courts were concerned. If the hon. member was aware of the representations which are coming to the Department of Justice at the present time concerning the other courts in Canada, perhaps he would admit that the provision is a sound one. However, I fully concur in the tribute which he has paid to the particular gentleman he has referred to.
This bill covers not only the case of a judge who has retired after having reached the age of 75, but of a judge who has resigned. Section 27 of the act reads:
Any judge who has heard the case and is absent at the delivery of judgment, may hand his opinion in writing to any judge present at the delivery of judgment, to be read or announced in open court, and then to be left with the registrar or reporter of the court.
The purpose of this bill is to allow a judge who has resigned his office, or who has been retired after having reached the age of 75, to be considered absent, within the meaning of this section, for a period of six months, so that he can give his opinion to any judge who may be present when the judgment is delivered.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to call
attention to one point made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), and direct the attention of the house to the fact that when the legislation was passed which compelled the retirement of a judge of the supreme court at the age of 75, the Minister of Justice was good enough to say that he would consider the matter before the event happened which would necessitate the retirement of the judge in question, especially as it affected his compensation. That judge undoubtedly has a contract with the state which entitles him to receive a salary for life or until such time as he resigns. New legislation has been enacted which limits
Supreme Court Act

his employment by the state merely because he has attained a given age without regard given to any consideration which he may urge. I think the government would be well advised to consider whether or not, in all cases of this kind where a contract has thus been amended, the judge should receive full salary. There are half a dozen cases which will be affected because I think there have been only two appointments made since the legislation in question was enacted. Undoubtedly one of the terms of these contracts governing new appointments is that they are subject to retirement at the age of 75 with the consequent pension which they will draw by reason of the services rendered up to the time of retirement. It may seem rather strange that attention should be directed to the matter in this way, but when a servant of the state, whether judicial or otherwise, has a contract with the state and we impose a new term in that contract, I think we must have regard to the terms and conditions under which the original contract was made. Although it may seem out of the ordinary that a judge should draw full salary when he is retired compulsorily, nevertheless, good faith and good morals, in my judgment, impose upon us that obligation and it is an obligation which we should not lightly disregard. I pointed that fact out to the minister when the other bill was under consideration, and when he speaks of parliament in its wisdom adopting that bill it must always be remembered that the wisdom of parliament consists of the majority of parliament. I do not believe that the Canadian people would approve of our departing from the general principle that the government must as in times past have respect for the sanctity of a contract made between a servant and the crown when 'he entered the employment of the state.

I had a resolution upon the order paper two years ago compelling the retirement of all judges, but the Minister of Justice rather forestalled me, and promised at that time that he would take the matter up with the provinces. I would like to ask the minister if he ever did that.

Duties of Hong Kong Official.
1.	To investigate all applications for visas made in accordance with subsection (e) of section 5 of the Chinese Immigration Act.
In the case of merchants this necessitates investigation of the firm in China to which applicant belongs to establish if applicant has sufficient capital investment and is connected with class of business such as would warrant classifying him as merchant within meaning of the act. (Merchant means a person devoting his undivided attention to mercantile pursuits, who has $2,500 gold or more invested in a business dealing exclusively in goods grown, produced or manufactured in China, or in exporting to China goods grown, produced or manufactured in Canada, and who has conducted such business for a period of at least three years. Restaurant keepers, laundry owners, rooming-house proprietors are not considered merchants.)
In the cases of students, our officer investigates their educational status and financial standing in order to establish if qualified to enter a Canadian university and if sufficient

funds are forthcoming to permit studying in such university without working in Canada during period of study.
2.	To check up vessels arriving from Canadian ports and identify Chinese deports for the purpose of establishing that they have really left Canada.
3.	To examine Chinese persons returning to Canada under outward registration (sections 23 and 24) for the purpose of establishing that after registration persons actually left Canada, and, further, are returning within the two year period as limited by statute.
4.	Passing on doubtful cases of other nationalities referred to the office by consular and other officials and by transportation companies.
Note.-Duties referred to in Nos. 2 and 3 are precautionary measures performed by our office owing to the fact that he is at Hong Kong, and are considered further safeguards in the general operation of the law.
Effect of having officer at Hong Kong.
1.	Prevents all inadmissible cases coming forward to Canadian ports of entry with re- ' sultant costly investigations, examinations and attempts to secure landing by court proceedings.
2.	Additional protection against fraud in returning registered Chinese.
3.	Lessening of number of applications at Pacific Coast ports of other nationals not admissible under Immigration regulations.

The province of British Columbia is not the only province which suffers from this Chinese immigration. To me the immigration policy of this government is a Chinese puzzle; as a matter of fact they have no immigration policy. We are only spending a little more than we did 30 years ago on this problem. In every city and town in Ontario the police commissions are having trouble with these people, who are taking the bread and butter out of the mouths of the women and girls of Ontario by doing domestic work. In Toronto the police commission have had trouble with the Chinese population all the time, particularly in connection with their restaurants. The minister talks about bonding them, but that does not mean a thing; a 78594-188J
bond will not check them up. What about the middlemen, the people who bring them here? Where do they come in? Conditions in Vancouver are such as to create a veritable Asiatic peril and it is a wonder the people do not rebel against such economic conditions resulting from the activities of so many orientals. In this vote the government provides $60,000 for salaries and contingencies in connection with Chinese immigration, but look at the next item; only $4,000 is provided for the relief of poor, distressed Canadians driven out of their own country by the immigration pblicy of the government. If the minister is equally good as Minister of Immigration and as Minister of Emigration, he will be very successful because he, by reason of the government policy, has driven out of this country 700,000 of our own people to seek work in the United States.
At a meeting held at Kingston of the general synod of the Church of England in Canada, representing all dioceses in this country, a resolution was passed dealing with this particular matter and with the immigration policy generally, and urging British immigration now being discriminated against. This government spends $400,000,000 yearly to maintain this country but they can find only $3,500,000 to spend on one of the greatest problems we have to face. Last night some hon. gentlemen wanted to reduce one of these votes by a million dollars; some western members say we have enough immigration; they are free traders with regard to industry in the east but protectionists when agriculture and their own home affairs are concerned.
I wish to protest against this item of $60,000 for salaries and contingencies in connection with Chinese immigration. I venture to say that hundreds of thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money is spent through the police departments of the country in checking up these people, and I know that in Toronto they take the bread and butter out of the mouths of our own poor women and girls. In the richer districts of Toronto, Hamilton and Winnipeg I have seen people engage Chinese to do their domestic work rather than pay a Canadian girl or woman a living wage. I say there should be a closed season for Chinese immigration for a period of five or ten years, or until such time as we may think it advisable to admit them again and give the British-born a chance.
Further, I desire to protest against the ianguage used by one of the western members of this house in referring to a bishop of the Church of England. Let me say that Bishop Lloyd fought with the Queen's

Own at Cut Knife in 1885, and did a great deal to save that great western country for the British Empire. He is not here to defend himself and We do not know whether or not the words quoted really came from him. When the Anglican synod of Canada met at Kingston two years ago they protested against the present policy of discrimination against British born immigrants. It brings to my mind the description by the poet William Cowper, when referring to the great fire of 1666 in the city of London he deplored the undue proportion of Europeans in the population of England. He declared that London was over-run with Europeans, and had become the common sewer of Paris and of Rome and had sucked in the dregs of all corrupted states.
We do not want that in Canada. A solution should be sought by the government for this great problem, but we will never be able to solve it while we have a free trader as commissioner of immigration. The first cornerstone of an immigration policy is to keep the people we have now and to provide work-provide an economic trade policy that will give jobs to British born immigrants: The government does not do that.
Seven hundred thousand of our men have gone to the United States and the government only provides $4,000 for the relief of distressed Canadians outside of Canada, while they ask us to vote $70,000 for Chinese immigration, an increase of $5,000 over last year. The minister's policy is nothing else but a Chinese puzzle; it has been one which retards immigration rather than encourages it. It is no wonder that- the British born in this country are beginning to wonder whether Canada is going to continue to be a British and a white man's country. Mr. Bruce in Australia is regulating this European and Asiatic immigration; he is going to make that country a white man's country. We are spending to-day on immigration $3,500,000, which is a million more than was spent in 1896, but we have not solved this problem of immigration and colonization. We might just as well close up the shop if the present policy is to be continued.
St. Catharines, Barrie, Belleville, Hamilton and other Canadian cities and towns are filled with Chinese labour and with Chinese restaurants. In some way these orientals have been able to get into Canada and to obtain licenses and they are forcing the white man's restaurant out of business. The women are being driven out of laundering, housekeeping, domestic work and the restaurant business, and their places are being taken by
(Mr. Church.]
Chinese labour. The government should declare a closed season and say that they will stop Chinese immigration for the next five or ten years or until such time as British immigration is brought up to a point more in keeping with the policy and traditions of a British dominion. The people of this country are beginning to wonder whether our country will continue to be British or whether it will soon be under the control of these Asiatics and Europeans. Time will tell. The economic policy of the government is driving Canadians to the States to look for jobs while the government brings in European and Asiatic immigrants to take their place.

My deputy informs me that the whole of this appropriation is scarcely ever spent. There is only a very small portion of it spent. This is to provide for assistance to bona fide Canadians who may happen to be stranded away from Canada or who may be in need of temporary financial help. Most of the oases occur in the British Isles and the expenses are under the control of the Director of European Emigration, London. In cases involving payment of transportation to Canada, for which we obtain a specially reduced rate, an undertaking of repayment is obtained from the person assisted, which repayment the department endeavours to collect from him upon his return to Canada, or from his parents or relatives if he happens to be unable to refund the money himself. The net expenditure for the fiscal year 1927-28, was $1,379.36, and the collections during that year amounted to $753.46, so that it is really an infinitesimal sum.

should be discussed when the labour estimates are under discussion. I have some inquiries to make with respect to it. I think my hon. friend from North Winnipeg will agree that this is a matter that comes under the Department of Labour.

These conductresses work in these buildings at St. John.

Ten years ago.

The first item is to

under agreement between the Department of Immigration and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The agreement was entered into ten years ago, nine payments have been made, and this is the last. It is difficult for me to give offhand all the details of a contract that was entered into ten years ago.

It appears to me that

I am sorry the Prime

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on two
former occasions when we were in committee I asked that vote 232 be called. The discussion in each case has centred around the health section. I would therefore suggest that we call vote 244, and that we complete the discussion on the section of health, and proceed to items under that section.
Item stands.
The administration of the acts respecting food and drugs, opium and narcotic drugs and proprietary or patent medicines, including the laboratory of hygiene, $150,000.

In the few remarks I made the other night I endeavoured to show the field of activity that was designed for this department, not only by the constitution but by the act that brought the department into being. Some of our friends opposite
have suggested that services which are now being rendered by the health department had previously been and could now be carried on by other departments of government. There is no doubt that that is true, but those who were responsible for the amalgamation of those services must have realized that there was a necessity for closer application on the part of those who were qualified to deal with them.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

I was indicating, Mr. Chairman, that under the old organization where the Department of Immigration controlled the medical inspection service that service was not efficiently performed, with the result that we introduced into Canada trachoma, which has spread as far west as among the Indians of British Columbia. We also found that our asylums were being filled with mentally deficient people; the hospitals were being filled; the charitable in-situtions were crowded by incompentents. Since the Department of Health has taken over that work I think I can say with certainty that conditions have very greatly improved, and this is due to the thorough inspection carried on. It is suggested thait the quarantine service could be oarried on under the Department of Immigration. As a matter of fact, that service at one time came under the Department of Agriculture, and we know from history that during that period many epidemics did originate from the quarantine stations. I am pleased to say that since the Health department has been in control of this service not one case has got through.
Regulations in relation to foods and drugs were formerly under the Department of Trade and Commerce, but since they have been placed under the Health department a considerable amount of research work has been done and the elimination of impurities from foods and drugs has been effected in great measure. The benefit which has resulted to the public from the health standpoint is inestimable. When it is realized to-day that scientific methods are followed in the preparation of foods, and that there has been a great evolution in this matter of refrigeration and in relation to the preserves that go into foods, many vegetable colourings being discarded and aniline dyes substituted for them, many of which dyes are poisonous, one can readily

Supply-Pensions and National Health
understand that a considerable amount of research and investigation is necessary in order properly to supervise the preparation of these products.

With respect to pure
food products, does the minister handle that branch of the public service?
Yes.
That is what the minister is speaking of just now?
Yes.

Perhaps the minister recalls the criticisms made by the producers of maple sugar and maple syrup in the province of Quebec as to what was done in the adulteration of some of their products. I understood that the government had taken action in this matter and also with respect to butter. Perhaps the minister, without interfering with the sequence of his remarks, will offer some observations in that regard.

We have a Maple Products Act whereby the Department of Health is empowered to take samples from the shelves, just as is done in connection with ordinary food products, and have these samples brought to the laboratories to be tested for purity. A pure maple product is required; that is the standard. A great deal of work has been done in this direction and some prosecutions have been entered into. There has been some complaint from the sugar producing districts in Quebec to the effect that the service has not been as efficient as it ought to be. I would point cut that the laboratory work in connection with maple products is one that requires probably the greatest degree of care, inasmuch as it is very easy to add cane and other sugars to these particular products, and the adulteration is very difficult of detection. The eld lead standard had been in vogue, but in practice it was found difficult to apply. In some districts that standard would run as high as 9 per cent, while in others and at other seasons, it might be as low as 1.5. That standard, therefore, is not altogether reliable, especially in view of the fact that there is a great variation in the districts in which the commodity is produced. It is true we have not as large an inspection service as we should like to have. If we had more inspectors we could bring more products in to be tested. Among the producers themselves there is a desire to turn out a pure product. 
The trouble comes after the producer has sold his product to the manufacturer; it is then that the adulteration occurs. We have, however, been successful in checking adulteration. I know of one firm's products having been taken from the shelf-one of the largest firms in Canada-and it was a good lesson to them. There has been a suggestion that the administration of the act might be better conducted under the Department of Agriculture, and that is under consideration.
Why?

Well, some of
those who made representations on the question thought that the Department of Agriculture was a little closer to the producer than the Health department and that consequently it could exercise greater control over the product at its source. I find, however, that in all probability the product is not very much disturbed at its source; it is after it leaves the point of production that adulteration takes place.
Perhaps it is easier for that department to get more inspectors.
I do not know about that.
They have 1,300 now.
I fancy cooperation would produce a better service. The control of culinary and drinking water on the great lakes has been taken up by the department.

Has it touched Ottawa
yet?

We have no jurisdiction in Ottawa, unfortunately, but on the great lakes and international waterways we have that jurisdiction and our service has been of considerable importance. For instance, typhoid fever was at one time a very common disease on ships on the great lakes;
I am pleased to say that last year there were only four cases of typhoid which were reported in that service. In the administration of the Proprietary and Patent Medicines Act, which was formerly under the Department of Trade and Commerce, there were sold at one time 60,000 preparations of this character; the number has been reduced to
6,000.	Many exaggerated and misleading claims have been disposed of and the public has been spared a good deal of money. It was never the intention of the Department of Health to merge the activities of the

Supply-Pensions and National Health
province iato a distinct unit, as has been suggested. But in cooperation with the provinces, through the Dominion Council of Health, we have been able to do work which I think has been quite effective.
The establishment of a research laboratory is desirable and I have no doubt that when the time is opportune such a laboratory will be established in Canada. But as I said the other night, the securing of a personnel for such a laboratory is more important than the expenditure of money in buildings and equipment. The government is not unwilling to provide money for the establishment of a laboratory of this character, but at present it would seem that the duties of the department in connection with the administration of the Food and Drugs Act occupy t'he present laboratory staff to the full, and the establishment of a research laboratory would mean the appointment of a staff of very considerable size with quarters of its own, together with a considerable outlay for equipment of a very expensive kind.
It was suggested to the committee that more money was being expended in connection with the health of animals than was spent in connection with the health of human beings. If my hon. friends would take into consideration the large sums of money spent by the provincial governments and the municipalities, together with the amount spent by the Dominion government in this regard, they would get a total expenditure of many millions of dollars. I have said, and I do not think it can be contradicted, that the Canadian people are making just as much progress in health matters as is being made by other countries throughout the world. We are fortunate, I think, in having, as deputy minister of the department a gentleman well known to health authorities not only in Canada but throughout the world as having exceptional knowledge of public health matters; I refer to Doctor Amyot.
The complaint has been made that the report of the department is too brief. That may be so, but a short study of the report does not give an accurate idea of the activities carried on or the amp unt of work done during the year. For instance, at page 10 Of the report it will be noticed that 416 samples of narcotic drugs were analysed during the year. One might write a book on the work done by the police under the supervision of the department in seizing 416 samples of these drugs and in the prosecutions which followed. In that regard I think we might say that in Canada the organization which controls the use of narcotic drugs is as efficient as any similar organization to be found anywhere in the world. The work last year was exceptionally well done, and we secured many convictions in the courts. I believe that to-day in New Westminster penitentiary there are over 60 people who have been sentenced to terms of from five to seven years for trafficking in these drugs, and the same situation prevails in Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal.
At page 33 of the report we find that patent medicines for cancer, diphtheria, diabetes, typhoid fever and other diseases are no longer permitted to be sold. That statement takes only a few lines, but it means that the public will be exploited no longer; it is a bald statement of fact. On page 39 we find that the total number of cases of typhoid on the great lakes during 1926 was only four. That is a brief statement also, but it means a great deal to those who know the character of that disease as it formerly existed on the great lakes before this service was undertaken. On page 47 of the report it will be noted that during the year 5,217 sailors were treated at Canadian ports. That statement means more than it indicates in words, but we can say that sailors coming to our shores receive treatment equal to if not better than that given by any other country in the world. That service is well organized in the larger ports of Canada, where we have officers under salary. In the smaller ports the customs officers act as our agents and where medical assistance is required it is furnished by local physicians either under fees or on a small salary basis.

That is particularly so
with regard to the quarantine stations, is it not?
The minister did not do anything about the infection of the oyster beds in Prince EdHvard Island?
We made an investigation some two or three years ago, when the epidemic came over here from the United States. Our officers were brought in at that time.

That was the typhoid
epidemic?
Yes, and at that time I think we made a health survey in Prince Edward Island as well.

I was referring to the
parasite which destroyed the oyster beds.

We had nothing
to do with that.
As I said, this laboratory tests the serums and vaccines and biological products. It is estimated that $10,000 of the $15,000 increase will foe required to carry on the increased inspection service at Montreal and Toronto; for the provision of scientific apparatus urgently needed to cope with the demands of advancement in food and drug work and to make replacements of certain laboratory apparatus which, in the course of time, has become either worn out or obsolete. An additional $5,000 will be required for investigations and prosecutions in connection with the traffic in narcotics. The amount voted in 1928-29 was $135,000, of which $134,956.39 was spent.

I think the minister's
statement has furnished additional proof, if any were necessary, for the statement I made the other evening that there is no originality and no initiative in this Department of Health, and there has been none since it was formed. Of course, if the minister is going to take credit for the work done by the provincial governments and the municipalities and for the preventive work of the mounted police he can make a very plausible statement, but 
when you get down to the real facts the minister has not been able to tell us of anything new which has been contributed by his department in order to preserve or improve the health of the people of this country. I have listened to the minister veiy carefully in my desire to secure some information or facts which would justify the existence of this department, but I have heard nothing of the kind. The minister has stated that he is going to hand back to the Department of Agriculture some of the work he took away from it-
I did not say that.
-evidently with the idea that the Department of Agriculture can do it better than the Department of Health. I can see no other reason.
I do not propose to let my hon. friend put words into my mouth which I have not used. He can make his own statement but he cannot make a statement for me.
I am in the judgment of the house if that is not a reasonable deduction to be taken from what the minister has said.
Not at all.

I stand to be corrected if the minister can produce any evidence to the contrary. But I say again that as far as doing anything to preserve or improve the national health of Canada, we have yet to learn of the first thing which this government has done. It is true that they have been inspecting some foods, some proprietary medicines and doing other routine work which was done in the past I think just as efficiently as it is being done to-day-in fact, I am credibly informed that it is being done by the same staff. If that be true, what right has the minister to assume that this work was neglected in the past?-because that is the only deduction we can draw from his remarks. That, I say, is about all the department has been doing.
There are many ^ays in which this government could improve the public health. Last Thursday night I referred to the great wastage of life and pointed out that in practically every instance the government had done nothing to improve conditions. The government might assist in the establishment of whole time county health offices. I think I am correctly informed when I say that the minister has absolutely refused to consider that proposition; he hides himself behind the

Supply-Pensions and National Health
British North America Act and states that the department is restricted to doing certain things. I have in my hand a letter given to me by the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) in which the statement is made that the minister refused absolutely to take that matter into consideration. It is undoubtedly within the power of the department to assist in the establishment of full time county medical health offices.
The minister has referred to what his department has done as regards quarantine, but I would direct his attention to the epidemics of rabies which occurred in the province of Ontario. I am not blaming the minister for that, because I know that matter comes under the Department of Agriculture, but it must be remembered that the disease entered this country from the United States; that it has caused the provincial government a great deal of alarm and has necessitated the expenditure of a considerable amount of money.
The minister referred also to the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and to the number of convictions which had been made under that act during the past year. I asked the government the following question:
How many persons were convicted last year for illegally selling any of the following drugs; opium, morphia, cocaine, or any of their derivatives?
If the minister's statement is correct, the answer which I received to that question must be wrong. According to the answer I received from the Deputy Minister of Health there were only 61 convictions in the whole Dominion of Canada, and I find that ten of that number were professional men of one kind or another. I aMo asked for the estimated number of drug addicts in Canada, and the answer was given as 8,000. If the statements made by the minister are correct, then I ask him: Where are those 8,000 adicts obtaining their drugs? The minister tells us that there has been a great diminution in the importation and sale of these drugs, but I find that there are still 8,000 people, according to the estimate made by his department, still using them, and only 61 convictions were made during the last twelve months.
We do not prosecute the addicts.

I would like to direct the attention of the house to some of the methods used by this department in dealing with this drug evil. I received a letter from a medical man in my district, who I believe is just as innocent of dealing in these drugs
as any hon. member in this house. If the name is necessary I will give it, but I do not think it is called for at the present time. He wrote as follows:
In regard to the conviction against me for breach of the Narcotic Act, I will give you the particulars as concisely as possible. Some time in August, 1926, Fraser called at my office and asked how much he owed me. He had broken into my office on three occasions, the last time being about three years before. He had done considerable damage, and stolen what morphia and syringes I had on hand, and some cash, and a sweater, possibly more. I asked him if his conscience was troubling him. He said that he was in very had shape at that time. He paid me $20 and I said that would do although it did not nearly cover me. He was dressed very neatly and I hardly knew him, as he changed so much in appearance. I asked him how hie was getting along and he said that after he was arrested in Gravenhurst he had been in an institution and had cut down to one-quarter the amount he had previously taken, and that he bad been out a year and had reduced to about one-fifth and was gradually reducing the amount. I gave him some good advice and warned Mm to be very careful, etc. He got up to go and then asked if I could spare him a few tablets. I replied that I did not know how many I had hut would look. I gave him about 20 tablets, gr. I each. The point is that I did not know the act, and did not think I was in error any more than if I dispensed a bottle of stomach mixture. I had never read the act, or ever received a copy of it. I considered I was giving medicine which I knew he required, and thought that I had a license to dispense. He came back on three more occasions, and I gave him tablets each time.
Some time in January, 1927, Miller a mounted police, came in and served me with the summons. I immediately called up T. N. Phelan, my solicitor in Toronto, and he was the first to inform me that I had committed a breach of the Narcotic Act, and advised me to settle if given the minimum fine of $200, and have the other charges withdrawn. This was done, and I paid $257.50.
I later had to appear before the council and nearly had a two months' suspension for infamous and disgraceful conduct, but got off with a severe reprimand.
I could not understand why the government sent a spotter down here to get me, unless I was using more morphia than the average physician. I bad never had an addict in for years before and only used it in the practice. No doubt you know that I have a good obstetric practice, and as a routine I left six morphine tablets after each case for after-pains, with instructions to burn the tablets that they did not use.
I think that is all that it is necessary for me to read1.
I am credibly informed that this is the common practice of the department, to send around their sleuths to try to catch the medical men who are ignorant of this act, bring them into the police court and have them fined. No one wants to pay a fine if he does not feel that he should pay it. An-
Supply-

-Pensions and National Health
other point is that once a physician is fined on a charge of that nature he is almost automatically barred from the practice of medicine; that is the serious part of it. I would ask the minister if this practice, which has been fairly general in the past, has been discontinued?

The hon. member was informed over a year ago that the department did not employ the type of investigator which is referred to in that letter. That incident happened back in 1926. The investigations to-day are conducted by the mounted police; the department does not send people in to pry upon the doctors.
What do they do?

When information comes to the department that some member of the medical profession is selling drugs, we make careful inquiries and if it is found that the statements are true, the man is investigated. If trafficking is discovered, he is brought into court, usually on a summary conviction if it is his first offence. If it is found that there has been regular trafficking and if he is what is known as a drug trafficker, he may be proceeded- against under indictment. That is the practice of the department and it will not be relinquished. But no medical man need get himself into trouble if he will comply with the act.
The minister cannot put up a straw man merely for the purpose of knocking it down. I was not referring to the trafficker.

Neither was I.
I was referring to the case -the hon. member mentioned, and the question he asked as to the procedure. I have given him the procedure now in vogue in the department. The hon. member for Kingston brought up a case and he had the idea that the department had proceeded hurriedly and without proper knowledge with regard to the matter.
Is the minister referring to the case I brought up?

Yes. We received information from Kingston that a certain medical man was supplying narcotics. That information, coming to the department, was investigated and the investigation brought forth a report.
Is the minister referring to the case I mentioned?

No. The report
was not satisfactory to the department, but 
later on the officer of the mounted1 police went into that doctor's office and bargained for narcotic drugs. "He found in the office supplies done up and addressed to parties in Ottawa for sale. Those packages were opened and drugs sold from them. That was the story. Our friends cannot complain if medical men get themselves into positions of that kind, but the department are not and have not been for the last two years, employing any addicts in their service.

There is no question as to the fact that the medical man was selling drugs, but it was found out that he was an irresponsible medical man who never should have been allowed to practise. When the time came, if attention bad not -been drawn to that fact, I am satisfied the -department would have proceeded against him with the usual prosecution instead of having him confined where he is now or where he was sent afterwards. The man was irresponsible; he should never have -been allowed to practise, but he was practising and he did not know what he was doing because he was under the influence of drags all the time. Surely the mounted policeman should have become acquainted with the type of medical man with whom he was dealing and said: This is not a case for prosecution; it is one for putting him in an institution; he is an addict himself.

I do not see how my hon. friend can take that stand. Our business was to check this man's traffic in narcotic drags. He had his own connections in Kingston and if it was known there that he was irresponsible and a fit subject for an institution, that surely is the duty of the local people. We did not intervene on that ground; we found that he was trafficking and trafficking for profit.

Does the minister
say that he would defend the prosecution of the man? Application was made a dozen times for his confinement in an institution.

We dealt with
the facts only as we found them.

But I would expect common sense to be used in connection with the prosecution. A mounted policeman should be a very good judge. This man has been in gaol -and detained in different institutions. It is not fair to say: We are going to prosecute him. I quite admit perhaps the department had no knowledge of that, but it certainly changed the prosecution- after the matter was drawn to its attention, and I will give the minister credit for that.

Supply-Pensions and National Health

We stayed the
prosecution.

I just want to make it
clear that the case we are now dealing with is not the one to which I referred.
No.

I am prepared to give
the minister all possible assistance in the house as well as out of it to prosecute criminals who are trafficking in these drugs, but he must exercise ordinary precautions not to stigmatize men whose reputations are clear. This is not the only case I have in my riding and in every case where they have been convicted, they have been convicted through ignorance of the law. I have had complaints from many parts of the province, and I am informed that the same course of action is still being pursued. I would be glad to have the minister's testimony that it is not.

The hon. member for
Muskoka-Ontario contends that the individual whose case he stated, was hardly used by the department. I cannot see this. Ignorance of the law, we are told, is no excuse, and certainly for the last twenty-five years I have understood thoroughly that it is against the law to give morphine to an addict.

Coming back to
the statement made by the minister and for information only, I should like the minister to tell us now what work was undertaken by his department to prevent or lessen typhoid on the great lakes?

We have required the owners of ships on the great lakes to furnish a separate water supply for culinary and drinking purposes. Formerly they took the water from the lake; now it comes from certified sources of supply. The tanks are inspected from time to time and samples of water taken. These samples are examined with the assistance of the laboratories of the provincial government; if things are not found to be in proper shape on the ship the owners are notified, and until repairs are made the ship does not sail. The water supply is being very carefully ohecked especially on the great lakes and on some of the western lakes. I have under my hand a chart giving the number of cases of typhoid as follows:
Number
Y ear	of cases
1923		 50
1924		 30
1925		 7
1926		 4
This shows a gradual decline since this system was inaugurated.
Of course the work of inspection there is largely provincial.
No, entirely under our direction.

The water supply
must be protected. I will come to that point a little later on. In regard to the food question, we are quite in sympathy with anything that will make for pure food, but last year I took up with the minister the question of sausages. The colouring substance which is and has been for years used to give the sausage a slight tint which makes it what it really is, has been acknowledged by the minister, his chemists and his department, to be non-in jurious.	Then what is the idea of
worrying the manufacturers of the sausage for using that colouring? Could some common sense not be used and the department say: This is not an injurious substance? On the other hand, if you are going to forbid its use, why permit its sale in shops and so forth? The department can say that the butcher, the manufacturer of sausages, is aware of this; that ignorance of the law is no excuse. But the butcher's trade is handed down from father to son and these men would like to know, because they have asked me, whether some change could not be made so that they could manufacture the sausages. The department is welcome to take care of the meats. This is not a preservative of meat. The minister admits that it is not, that it is simply used for colouring, and that it is used in connection with a cheap food entering into the dietary of a great many people. If there is any argument in favour of continuing the prosecutions for the use of colouring matter, I would like to know what it is.

The department are of the opinion that if the people desire to eat sausage meat, they should have a pure product. It is welll-known that in the better abattoirs and better shops, where meat is properly taken care of and there is proper refrigeration and care in handling, meat can be kept fresh and will make sausages that will stand up. On November 4, 1922, he was examined by Dr. Elliott who ascribed his condition to gas poisoning and estimated his disability at 35 pet' cent minus 10. Dr. Seaton also estimated his disability at 25 per cent. Dr. Leonard Murray on May 23, 1923, diagnosed a mitral insufficiency and Dr. Elliott again on May 23. 1925, diagnosed his condition as chronic gas poisoning and reaffirmed his statement that the man's disability was about 35 per cent.
Dootor Elliott in 1925 diagnosed the man's condition the same as he did before, namely, gas poisoning with a disability of 35 per cent. In 1924, after the Board of Pension Commissioners had refused to accept him as a disability case, the matter was taken up before one of the members of the federal appeal board, who decided in favour of the soldier, that be was suffering from a disability received on service. That decision of the federal appeal board was contested by the Board of Pension Commissioners, who appealed the case to a quorum of the federal appeal board. The quorum of the board decided again in favour of the soldier, stating that he had a disability due to service. The point is that the man having tried for a number of years before the Board of Pension Commissioners to get a pension, after the federal appeal board gave the decision and after the appeal was decided in his favour, they granted him a 20 per cent disability and paid him on that basis. After he had received that pension of 20 per cent for a short time, I hardly know how long, the Board of Pension Commissioners had him reexamined' and reduced his .pension to 10 per cent. At that time I took his case up with the Board of Pension Commissioners and had him reexamined. I also secured from his

Supply-Pensions and National Health
employer a statement with regard to his condition and the number of days he had lost. This is what the employer said:
The above has shown us a letter from you ashing him to obtain from his employer the amount of time he has lost through disabilities.
He has lost a total of 201 hours during the year 1925.
We would like to go further and state that this man is married with two children, and is of an ambitious type. Since coming from overseas, he has been unable to do manual labour where any physical exertion was needed, and even on the work he is doing, at times is plainly working on his nerve. We have known this man as an employee for several years, both before and since the war, and his ambition to keep going in spite of his disabilities has earned our admiration.
These are the points in connection with this case. He undoubtedly is suffering from chronic gas poisoning. Let me read the symptoms as described in Major General Sir William MacFherson's book in regard to the medical services in the war, published in 1923. He says at page 402:
Commonest feature-prolonged inability for severe muscular effort or even moderate exercise. associated with taehy cardia and rapid shallow breathing.
The men's wind was gone and to some extent their nerves.
This is exactly what this man said. Among the other effects are giddiness on standing, headaches, and general vascular instability. This man complained of dizziness.
It was closely allied to disordered action of the heart.
Mild bronchitis in about 15 per cent of all cases.
The only part of this man's disability for which he is receiving a pension is chronic bronchitis due to gas poisoning. Among the other symptoms of gas poisoning I quote:
Disordered heart action-irritable heart, precordial pain, exhaustion, dyspnoea, persistent taehy cardia after exercise, in one-third of total.
Spasmodic nocturnal "asthena" either alone or in conjunction with irritable heart in less than a third.
Exercise caused intense headache, giddiness and slow pulse (abnormally).
Thirty-five per cent of the above cases after three months' treatment persisted and were sent home for prolonged treatment, One group was composed of those who had not (apparently been gravely gassed. I quote again:
Condition supposed to be due to thickening of pulmonary epilhelium and bronehilitis obliterans.
Causing deficient oxygenation of the blood similar to that found at high altitudes.
Every medical man who has examined this soldier stated that he has the symptoms of chronic gas poisoning, but they have not
stated that he is suffering from chronic gas poisoning. Doctor Murray said that he had fibrosis of the lung, which follows the description given by Major General MacPherson- shortness of breath; those are exactly the words that Major General MacPherson uses. The man is admitted to be suffering from chronic bronchitis, which is found in almost thirty-five per cent of the gas poisoning cases, and yet the pension board will recognize only one symptom of gas poisoning, refusing to accept the other symptoms of gas poisoning as due to service, and those other symptoms are those of which the man complains most and which keep him from doing his work properly. Why the board and the department-
Not the department.
Has the department ever taken it up with the board?
We have referred the case to the board, I presume, with whatever arguments my hon. friend presented. We do not advise the board as to their judgments.

Here is a
case where for three or four years the board absolutely refused to acknowledge that the man had any disability whatever.

I am very sorry
to hear that.

After the man had got the decision of the appeal board the pension board absolutely refused to accept any symptom of gas poisoning except chronic bronchitis, although the other symptoms are present showing that the man is suffering from chronic gas poisoning. I would ask the minister to take this case up with the board and see if they cannot 'be influenced to give to this man better consideration than he has so far received. I might add that I have this case before the board now. I asked to have this man brought before a board in the city of Toronto to consider whether his other symptoms could not be regarded as establishing chronic gas poisoning, so that he could be given consideration for that disability. He had been receiving free treatment for chronic bronchitis, but not for the symptoms of chronic gas poisoning.

I shall be glad
to bring the case to the attention of the board with the remarks which my hon. friend has made.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Pensions and National Health
Unemployment relief, $250,000.
Mr, CAMPBELL:	How has this money
been spent?

This expenditure
is made by the board to those who are pensioners for disabilities incurred while on service, to those who have received a final payment by agreement, and to former members of His Majesty's forces, provided, however, that the disabled members of the imperial forces arriving in Canada not subsequent to December, 1924. Assistance is provided in winter where investigation indicates that distress would be occasioned if help were not forthcoming. Help is given to single men at the rate of $30 per month; man and wife, S45, man and wife and one child, $57; man and wife and two or more children, $67. Assistance is granted in kind in the form of orders on the local grocers, coal dealers, bakers, and so forth.

How much was spent
last year?
The amount spent was $378,000.

Item agreed to.
Operating expense and working capital, $300,-
000.

What is the reason for
this increase of $10,000?

Contingent expenses of the board which heretofore were paid out of a separate vote granted to the commissioners are included in this appropriation. In other words, we have taken in $10,000 that was formerly paid out of their vote.

What is working capital
in a case of this kind?
Office supplies and expenses, telephone and telegraph, travelling expenses, stationery, motor transport, advertising, transportation of staff, and so forth. The expenditure last year was $271,000.

Item agreed to.
Employers' liability compensation, $75,000.
How does this come under this department instead of the Department of Labour?

The vote is used for this purpose: Where a pensioner seeking employment goes to an employer, and the employer says, "You are disabled; you are a bad risk in my mill; I shall probably have to pay a compensation fee," the government

assumes the payment of the compensation awarded by a Workmen's Compensation Board in the case of injury to the pensioner of 25 per cent and upwards who gets employment under those conditions. It is a very good provision and has been in operation for some years. The amount spent last year was about $20,000.

Item agreed to.
Sheltered employment, $175,000.
What is sheltered employment?

These are the
veteraft shops in Halifax, Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Victoria.

Item agreed to.
Federal appeal board, $130,000.
To whom does the federal appeal board report, or does it make a report?
They make a report to the Minister of Justice.
Has it been brought down yet?
I do not know.
Is it in printed form?
I think so.
In the report of the Department of Pensions and National Health naturally you look for some details with regard to the appeal board, bult it ds impossible to find any.
I shall be glad to get my friend a copy of the report.
It is not even indexed. The only reference either in the estimates or in this report is that the amount is $130,000.
I will make inquiry and leit my hon. friend have the report.
Is one printed each year?
I think so but I cannot say for certain. I believe it was tabled early in the session.

I asked the minister the same question last year, and he was not able to give any information. It is the most natural thing in the world to read the report of the Pensions department in an endeavour to ascertain what the board is doing, but it is impossbile to find anything about it in the report.
I shall be glad to give my hon. friend the information.
